c.tagline: New Zealand's windy, walkable capital of coffee, craft beer and creativity.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered; major operators include Wellington Combined Taxis and Green Cabs, and ride-hailing apps are widely used from the airport and CBD.

emergency.note: 111 is the single emergency number for police, fire and ambulance across New Zealand.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Courtenay Place can get rowdy with drunken crowds late on weekend nights.

hood_desc: The lively southern half of the CBD, packed with restaurants, bars, craft-beer taprooms, apartments and galleries; best for first-timers who want the city's dining and nightlife on their doorstep.
Wellington's bohemian pedestrian spine of vintage shops, cafes, live-music venues and the famous Bucket Fountain; suits travellers who want arty, indie character and a buzzing night scene.

A leafy, hilly residential suburb of Victorian cottages just east of the CBD, ringed by the Town Belt and topped by the Mount Victoria Lookout; good for those wanting calm, greenery and harbour views.
An upscale waterfront suburb along the harbour with a golden-sand beach, seaside promenade and Art Deco apartments; suits travellers wanting scenic walks and a relaxed, elegant base near the water.
Wellington's oldest suburb, home to Parliament, Old St Paul's, the Katherine Mansfield House and grand timber villas; ideal for visitors drawn to history, heritage architecture and civic landmarks.

water.note: Tap water is safe and high quality.

transit.hours: Buses and trains run roughly 6am to around midnight, with limited weekend 'After Midnight' late-night buses; there is no true 24-hour network, so taxis or rideshare cover the small hours.
transit.note: Metlink coordinates the region's buses, trains and harbour ferry; the historic Wellington Cable Car (Lambton Quay to Kelburn) is a separate scenic service popular with visitors.
transit.pay: Visitors tap on/off buses, trains and the harbour ferry with a Snapper card (sold at convenience stores, the Snapper website or app) loaded with cash; contactless bank card and mobile pay is being rolled out across the network. The Wellington Cable Car is paid separately.

tip.r: Not expected; hospitality staff are paid a full wage. Rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% for exceptional service is appreciated but uncommon.

food.name: Whitebait fritter
food.desc: Tiny translucent inanga bound in a light egg batter and pan-fried, served with lemon and white bread - a short, prized spring season.

places.name: Whitebait

places.name: Ortega Fish Shack

food.desc: New Zealand shellfish at its simplest: plump green-lipped mussels steamed in wine, and Bluff oysters raw when the season allows.

places.name: Ortega Fish Shack

places.name: Shed 5

food.desc: Blue cod, tarakihi or gurnard in crisp batter with hand-cut chips - eaten out of paper on the waterfront or Island Bay seafront.

places.name: The Chippery

places.name: Wellington Trawling Sea Market

places.name: Ortega Fish Shack

food.name: New Zealand meat pie
food.desc: Short pastry filled with steak and cheese, mince or lamb - the national handheld lunch, best eaten hot enough to burn your fingers.

places.name: Puku
places.note: Opened in 2025 with a homemade-tasting classic pie; already a Wellington cult favourite.

places.name: Leeds Street Bakery

places.name: Pandoro Panetteria
places.note: Long-established Wellington bakery, good for pies plus sourdough on the way out.

food.name: Peanut butter treats
food.desc: Wellington is home to Fix and Fogg, so peanut butter turns up on toast, in cookies and in ice cream all over town.

places.name: Moore Wilson's Fresh
places.note: Wellington's best-loved food hall; the place to buy Fix and Fogg jars and other local pantry goods.

places.name: Leeds Street Bakery
places.note: Bakes peanut-butter-laced cookies and slices; sits in the same laneway food cluster.

places.name: Customs Brew Bar
places.note: Coffee-first cafe from Coffee Supreme where a peanut butter toast order is a Wellington ritual.

food.name: Hokey pokey ice cream
food.desc: Vanilla ice cream shot through with shards of honeycomb toffee - a New Zealand invention, best eaten walking the waterfront.

places.name: Kaffee Eis
places.note: Gelato kiosk on the Oriental Parade seafront, a Wellington summer institution.

places.name: Gelissimo Gelato
places.note: Waterfront gelateria near the lagoon making small batches daily, including local flavours.

places.name: Moore Wilson's Fresh
places.note: Stocks New Zealand ice cream brands if you want a tub rather than a cone.

food.name: Flat white
food.desc: Wellington's defining drink: a double ristretto under thin, glossy steamed milk. The city has one of the world's densest cafe scenes.

places.name: Havana Coffee Works
places.note: Roastery cafe in a corrugated-iron warren; one of the roasters that built Wellington coffee.

places.name: Customs Brew Bar
places.note: Coffee Supreme's flagship bar on Ghuznee Street, serious about extraction and single origins.

places.name: Peoples Coffee
places.note: Fair-trade roaster with a neighbourhood cafe that locals treat as a second living room.

food.name: Wellington craft beer
food.desc: The self-styled craft beer capital of New Zealand - hazy IPAs, pilsners and wild experiments poured a few streets from where they are brewed.

places.name: Garage Project Taproom
places.note: Cult brewery on Aro Street; the taproom pours experimental one-offs you cannot get elsewhere.

places.name: Rogue and Vagabond
places.note: Huge rotating tap list, pizza and coffee-sack beanbags on the grass outside.

places.name: Golding's Free Dive
places.note: Tiny, wildly decorated Leeds Street bar with a sharply curated New Zealand tap list.

landmarks: The Beehive (NZ Parliament Buildings)
New Zealand's distinctive, cone-shaped executive wing of Parliament is one of the most photographed and instantly recognizable government buildings in the world.
Te Papa Tongarewa (Museum of New Zealand)
The nation's free flagship museum on the waterfront blends Māori and Pacific culture, natural history, and interactive exhibits in a striking harbourside building.
Wellington Cable Car
This historic funicular climbs from downtown to the Botanic Garden, rewarding riders with sweeping views over the city and harbour.
Mount Victoria Lookout
The single best panoramic vantage point over Wellington city, harbour, and surrounding hills, especially magical at sunset.
Zealandia Ecosanctuary
A pioneering fenced urban wildlife reserve where rare native birds like kākā and tuatara roam freely just minutes from the CBD.
Oriental Bay
Wellington's glittering waterfront beach promenade, lined with palm trees and pōhutukawa, is the city's postcard seaside strip.
Old St Paul's
A beautifully preserved 19th-century Gothic Revival timber church whose intricate wooden interior is a beloved architectural gem.
Wellington Botanic Garden
25 hectares of native forest, rose gardens, and colourful seasonal displays with a historic cable car link and hilltop views.
Cuba Street & Bucket Fountain
Wellington's quirky, bohemian shopping strip is anchored by the whimsical, water-splashing Bucket Fountain, a favorite photo stop.
Wellington Waterfront
A lively promenade of boardwalks, public art, and cafes framing the harbour, capturing the relaxed, maritime character of the capital.

train.note: Everything arrives at Wellington Railway Station at the northern end of Lambton Quay, a few minutes' walk from the CBD. The Northern Explorer runs to Auckland about three days a week and takes roughly 11 hours through the volcanic plateau; the Te Reo Hurihuri Capital Connection runs once each way daily from Palmerston North, and the Wairarapa Line serves Masterton about five times a day. Four electrified suburban lines cover the Hutt Valley, Kapiti Coast, Johnsonville and Melling on Metlink's Snapper card. New Zealand has no land borders and therefore no international trains.

bus.note: InterCity (https://www.intercity.co.nz/) coaches arrive and depart from Platform 9 at Wellington Railway Station, which keeps bus, train and ferry transfers within a couple of hundred metres of each other. Daily services run to Palmerston North (about 2.5 hrs), Napier, Taupo, Rotorua and on to Auckland (about 11 hrs), and advance online saver fares are far cheaper than buying on the day. Regional and city buses are run under the Metlink brand (https://www.metlink.org.nz/). No coach service crosses an international border from New Zealand.

intl.to: Picton (New Zealand) - sails from the Kaiwharawhara terminal, about 3 km north of the city with a free shuttle from the railway station
Picton (New Zealand) - sails from Waterloo Quay, a short walk from the railway station
Days Bay, Seatoun & Matiu/Somes Island (New Zealand) - from Queens Wharf in the CBD

ferry.note: The Cook Strait crossing to Picton takes about 3-3.5 hours and both operators run several sailings a day in each direction, including overnight departures. Interislander uses the Kaiwharawhara terminal with a free shuttle bus from the railway station, while Bluebridge berths on Waterloo Quay within walking distance of it. Cars, campervans and cabins need booking well ahead over the December-February holidays, and sailings are occasionally cancelled in strong southerly gales, so leave slack in an itinerary. Inside the harbour, East by West runs commuter and scenic ferries from Queens Wharf, including the electric Ika Rere. There are no international ferry services from New Zealand.

half.name: Martinborough
half.blurb: Martinborough is a wine village across the Remutaka Range known for Pinot Noir vineyards clustered around a small town square.

half.name: Kapiti Island
half.blurb: Kapiti Island is a predator-free nature reserve reached by boat, home to native birds like kiwi and takahe.

half.name: Cape Palliser
half.blurb: Cape Palliser has a lighthouse atop steep cliffs and a colony of New Zealand fur seals on the rocks below.

full.name: Picton and Marlborough Sounds
full.blurb: Picton sits across Cook Strait on the South Island, reached by ferry through the scenic Marlborough Sounds.
